title: Antiochus Epiphanes (Daniel) and the man of sin (Paul): such predictions require certain knowledge of contingents
source_text: VII. His addi possunt quae leguntur apud Danielem praedicta de Antiochi Epiphanis impietate, superbia, libidine, & saevitia, qua in Judaeos grassaturus erat, & ipsum Dei templum profanaturus. Itemque apud Paulum de adventu filii illius perditionis qui in templo Dei sessurus, & supra ipsum Deum se elaturus erat, plurimosque in errorem mendacibus signis inducturus. Quae omnia cum ab hominibus libere patranda fuerint, a Dei spiritu in scripturis loquente, certo, clare, & sigillatim, uti factum videmus, praedici non potuerunt, nisi Deus omnium futurorum eventuum, quantumlibet contingentium, certam & distinctam notitiam habeat.
pass_a_gloss: To these can be added what are read foretold in Daniel of the impiety, pride, lust, and cruelty of Antiochus Epiphanes, with which he was going to rage against the Jews, and profane the very temple of God. And likewise in Paul of the coming of that son of perdition who was going to sit in the temple of God, and exalt himself above God himself, and lead very many into error by lying signs. All which since they were to be done freely by men, could not be foretold by the spirit of God speaking in the scriptures, certainly, clearly, and one by one, as we see was done, unless God has a certain and distinct knowledge of all future events, however contingent.
pass_b_english: To these may be added what Daniel foretells of the impiety, pride, lust and cruelty of Antiochus Epiphanes, with which he would rage against the Jews and profane God's own temple. Paul likewise foretells the coming of the son of perdition, who would sit in God's temple, exalt himself above God himself, and lead very many astray by lying signs.

All these things were to be done freely by human beings. The Spirit of God, speaking in Scripture, could not have foretold them certainly, clearly and one by one, as we see was done, unless God has certain and distinct knowledge of all future events, however contingent they may be.

choices.why: The Schools' term for future events without a necessary and determinate cause; kept as a technical term.
